background.definition: Cryptosporidiosis is a parasitic disease that causes diarrheal symptoms in all age groups. Symptoms usually last 1 to 2 weeks in healthy individuals and longer in the immunocompromised.

list.listitem: There are approximately 2.6 cases/100,000 persons/year.
It is estimated that 750,000 American are affected each year. Cryptosporidium parvum is associated with animal exposure in rural areas, while Cryptosporidium hominis is more common in urban areas.

Cryptosporidium prevalence in a pool of 51,123 HIV-positive patients is estimated to be 10.0 to 26.3% depending upon which test method is used. Ten percent if stain microscopy used, Antigen detection method is high as 26.3%.
Incidence in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia may be as high as 78% in the first two years of life.
Worldwide, it estimated that there were 44.8 million cases of diarrhea in children younger than 5 years old.
Cryptosporidium causes 2.2% to 12% of episodes of diarrhea in immunocompetent persons in high resource countries.
A systematic review found somewhat higher prevalences when molecular methods were used to detect cryptosporidium of 9% to 21%.
Cryptosporidium is one of the most common causes of waterborne disease in humans worldwide.
Estimates suggest over 202,000 attributable deaths per year due to Cryptosporium in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia each year, mostly in children.
In childeren under 5 years of age, each episode results in significant decrease in height-for-age, weight-for-age, and weight-for-height Z scores.
Less common subspecies—C. felis, C. ubiquitum, and C. tyzzeri
In low and middle income countries, crosded living conditions, animal contacxt, and open defecation are the most important risk factors for cryptosporidium infection.
The waterborne parasites, Cryptosporidium parvum and hominis, live in the small intestine of infected humans and animals.
The parasite spreads through the fecal-oral route.
Infection results in villous atrophy and crypt hypertrophy. This results in malabsorption of food and hypersecretion of the intestinal tissue.
Primary prevention is to avoid fecal-oral transmission through proper hygiene. C
Once infected, secondary prevention is to avoid recreational waters for at least 2 weeks after diarrhea stops. C
Rifabutin reduces the risk of contracting cryptosporidiosis in patients with advanced HIV infection.C
Water filters in the home can decrease the presence of cryptosporidium in the water supply in low income countries.C
Suspect cryptosporidiosis in patients with significant diarrheal illness, especially if immunocompromised. C

Order confirmatory testing with direct fluorescent antigen detection or enzyme immunoassay for Cryptosporidium. PCR tests for patients with severe and/or prolonged diarrhea can confirm the species to help identify the source.C

list.listitem: In patients with persistent or severe diarrhea, take a careful history of exposure to contaminated water such as swimming pools, lakes, hot tubs, and streams. If an immunocompromised patient develops diarrhea, strongly consider cryptosporidiosis.

Symptoms typically begin 2 to 10 days (average 7 days) after exposure to Cryptosporidium parasites. The most common symptom is watery diarrhea; other symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, fever, dehydration, and weight loss.
Diarrhea usually lasts 1 to 2 weeks, but intermittent symptoms can last up to 30 days in healthy individuals and even longer in immunocompromised individuals (e.g. HIV).

In a large outbreak of Cryptosporidium in Milwaukee in 1993, the median duration of disease was 9 days and patients had a median of 12 stools per day. Frequency of symptoms was as follows: watery diarrhea in 93%, abdominal cramps in 84%, weight loss in 75%, fever in 57%, and vomiting in 48%.
If cryptosporidiosis is suspected based on clinical history, send stool specimens to be tested for specifically for Cryptosporidium.

Three tests are readily available in most labs to test for Cryptosporidium: modified acid fast stain, direct fluorescent antibody test, or enzyme immunoassays. Newer PCR tests are more sensitive than other tests, but are not as readily available. Acid fast stain of a single specimen is very sensitive and specific in AIDS patients with diarrhea.
The CerTest Crypto rapid diagnostic test was only 50% sensitive and 93% specific (PV+ 61%, PV- 88%) in a study down in sub-Saharan Africa.

Low cost LED microscopy with auramine staining was 88% sensitive and 99% specific in comparison with PCR in a study of children in Ethiopia with diarrhea. The same study found that an inexpensive immunochromatographic lateral-flow assays (ICLF) not requiring refrigeration was similarly accurate.
A new dot hybridization assay (sensitivity 95% and specificity 99%) may be helpful in routine investigation of large number of samples.
Routine ova and parasite testing does not identify Cryptosporidium.

In a known sample of 40 positive Cryptosporidium homnis and Crytosporium parvum specimens, RT-PCR detected 40/40 specimens, acid fast microsopy detected 20/40 specimens, antigen-based testing detected 21/40 specimens, and a GI panel detected 33/40 specimens.
See for a suggested approach to management.
Most immunocompetent patients recover with only supportive treatment including oral or IV rehydration. C
Nitazoxanide is recommended for immunocompetent patients with protracted or severe illness (NNT = 2), but is not helpful for immunocompromised patients. A
For persons with AIDS, maximizing antiretroviral treatment is the treatment of choice. B

Nitazoxanide is effective in treating immunocompetent patients with significant symptoms. In one study of 90 outpatients randomized to receive nitazoxanide 500 mg twice daily for 3 days, clinical response rates were 96% versus 41% (NNT = 2). Other studies have confirmed this benefit in adults and children.

However, nitazoxanide does not appear to be effective in immunocompromised patients. For immunocompromised patients with AIDS, antiretroviral treatment is the treatment of choice. Nitazoxanide does reduce oocyte shedding in immunocompromised patients, which may reduce their infectivity to other people. Paromomycin (NNT = 1) and azithromycin (NNT = 2.6) may also reduce oocyte shedding in immunocompromised patients.

A small pilot study randomized 64 infants with diarrhea caused by cryptosporidosis to nitazoxanide, nitazoxanide + probiotic, or supportive care but found no difference in the duration of infection. However, it may have been underpowered.
Antidiarrheal agents such as kaopectin and loperamide may reduce symptoms.
Most healthy patients will recover without treatment.
Oral rehydration is sufficient for most patients.
IV hydration for severely dehydrated patients may be necessary.
Consider infectious disease consultation if the patient is immunocompromised.
Immunocompetent patients usually recover in 1 to 2 weeks without treatment. C
Cryptosporidiosis can be life-threatening in immunocompromised patients and infants, in whom it typically takes a more protracted course. C

A systematic review of 15 studies in industrialized countries found that long term sequelae including chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, fatigue, and weight loss occurred in about 25% of persons in observational studies, and that chronic diarrhea was 6 times more likely following infection with cryptosporidiosis at 28 months.
Pregnant women are at a higher risk of dehydration. They need to maintain oral hydration.
Infants are at a higher risk of dehydration and life-threatening illness. Maintaining oral hydration is important.

Nitazoxanide is effective in immunocompetent but not immunocompromised children (NNT = 2). Pediatric dosing for age 1 to 3 years is 100 mg po twice daily for 3 days, and for age 4 to 11 years is 200 mg po twice daily for 3 days.

If patient is not responding, consider infectious disease consult. Nitazoxanide, Paromomycin. or azithromycin may improve symptoms and oocyte shedding, but may not cure.
Correct underlying cause of immunodeficiency, rehydration.
Symptomatic therapy with oral or IV rehydration. Nitazoxanide optional.
